name: Pennsylvania

events.title: Ratified the Constitution
events.text: Pennsylvania ratified the Constitution on December 12, 1787, the 2nd state to do so. The Constitution gave it 8 seats in the House until the first census.

events.title: Statewide (general ticket) elections
events.text: In the 1st Congress (1789–1791), Pennsylvania elected all of its representatives statewide on a general ticket instead of by district.

events.title: 1790 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1790 census, Pennsylvania's House delegation grew from 8 to 13 seats.

events.title: Statewide (general ticket) elections
events.text: In the 3rd Congress (1793–1795), Pennsylvania elected all of its representatives statewide on a general ticket instead of by district.

events.title: 1800 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1800 census, Pennsylvania's House delegation grew from 13 to 18 seats.

events.title: 1810 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1810 census, Pennsylvania's House delegation grew from 18 to 23 seats.

events.title: 1820 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1820 census, Pennsylvania's House delegation grew from 23 to 26 seats.

events.title: 1830 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1830 census, Pennsylvania's House delegation grew from 26 to 28 seats.

events.title: 1840 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1840 census, Pennsylvania's House delegation shrank from 28 to 24 seats.

events.title: 1850 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1850 census, Pennsylvania's House delegation grew from 24 to 25 seats.

events.title: 1860 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1860 census, Pennsylvania's House delegation shrank from 25 to 24 seats.

events.title: 1870 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1870 census, Pennsylvania's House delegation grew from 24 to 27 seats.

events.title: Some members elected at-large
events.text: In the 43rd Congress (1873–1875), Pennsylvania elected 3 of its representatives statewide (at-large) and the rest by district.

events.title: 1880 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1880 census, Pennsylvania's House delegation grew from 27 to 28 seats.

events.title: Some members elected at-large
events.text: In the 48th through 50th Congresses (1883–1889), Pennsylvania elected one of its representatives statewide (at-large) and the rest by district.

events.title: 1890 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1890 census, Pennsylvania's House delegation grew from 28 to 30 seats.

events.title: Some members elected at-large
events.text: In the 53rd through 57th Congresses (1893–1903), Pennsylvania elected 2 of its representatives statewide (at-large) and the rest by district.

events.title: 1900 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1900 census, Pennsylvania's House delegation grew from 30 to 32 seats.

events.title: 1910 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1910 census, Pennsylvania's House delegation grew from 32 to 36 seats.

events.title: Some members elected at-large
events.text: In the 63rd through 67th Congresses (1913–1923), Pennsylvania elected 4 of its representatives statewide (at-large) and the rest by district.

events.title: 1930 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1930 census, Pennsylvania's House delegation shrank from 36 to 34 seats.

events.title: 1940 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1940 census, Pennsylvania's House delegation shrank from 34 to 33 seats.

events.title: Some members elected at-large
events.text: In the 78th Congress (1943–1945), Pennsylvania elected one of its representatives statewide (at-large) and the rest by district.

events.title: 1950 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1950 census, Pennsylvania's House delegation shrank from 33 to 30 seats.

events.title: 1960 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1960 census, Pennsylvania's House delegation shrank from 30 to 27 seats.

events.title: 1970 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1970 census, Pennsylvania's House delegation shrank from 27 to 25 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 1980 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1980 census, Pennsylvania's House delegation shrank from 25 to 23 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 1990 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1990 census, Pennsylvania's House delegation shrank from 23 to 21 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 2000 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2000 census, Pennsylvania's House delegation shrank from 21 to 19 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: Vieth v. Jubelirer
events.text: Voters challenged Pennsylvania's 2002 congressional map as a partisan gerrymander. The Supreme Court rejected the claim, with a plurality finding no workable standard for deciding such cases.

events.title: 2010 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2010 census, Pennsylvania's House delegation shrank from 19 to 18 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: League of Women Voters v. Commonwealth
events.text: In January 2018 the Pennsylvania Supreme Court ruled that the 2011 congressional map violated the state constitution's Free and Equal Elections Clause. The court adopted its own map in February 2018, used from that year's election.

events.title: 2020 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2020 census, Pennsylvania's House delegation shrank from 18 to 17 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: Court picks a map
events.text: When the legislature and governor did not agree on a map, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court chose one in February 2022 in Carter v. Chapman.

compactnessNote: Polsby-Popper compactness (4π × area ÷ perimeter²) measured on the projected district shapes. It describes shape only: coastlines, rivers and county lines lower it too, so a low score is not evidence of intent. "Irregular" marks the least compact 5% of district shapes in each census era nationally.

c002.text: Pennsylvania elected its House members statewide on a general ticket in 1788. For the 2nd Congress it elected them from districts instead.

c003.text: After the 1790 census changed Pennsylvania's seats from 8 to 13, Pennsylvania still elected all of its members statewide, so it had no districts to redraw.

c004.text: Pennsylvania went back to a statewide general ticket for the 3rd Congress. In 1794 it returned to electing members from districts.

c008.text: New map drawn after the 1800 census, which raised Pennsylvania's seats from 13 to 18. It was first used in the 1802 election.

c013.text: New map drawn after the 1810 census, which raised Pennsylvania's seats from 18 to 23. It was first used in the 1812 election.

c018.text: New map drawn after the 1820 census, which raised Pennsylvania's seats from 23 to 26. It was first used in the 1822 election.

c023.text: New map drawn after the 1830 census, which raised Pennsylvania's seats from 26 to 28. It was first used in the 1832 election.

c027.text: Not a new map: the historical boundary records show only slight differences in 2 districts from the previous Congress, and no statewide redistricting is recorded for this election.

c028.text: New map drawn after the 1840 census, which cut Pennsylvania's seats from 28 to 24. It was first used in the 1842 election.

c030.text: Not a new map: the historical boundary records show only slight differences in 2 districts from the previous Congress, and no statewide redistricting is recorded for this election.

c033.text: New map drawn after the 1850 census, which raised Pennsylvania's seats from 24 to 25. It was first used in the 1852 election.

c038.text: New map drawn after the 1860 census, which cut Pennsylvania's seats from 25 to 24. It was first used in the 1862 election.

c044.text: New map drawn after the 1870 census, which raised Pennsylvania's seats from 24 to 27. It was first used in the 1874 election.

c045.text: Not a new map: the historical boundary records show only slight differences in 2 districts from the previous Congress, and no statewide redistricting is recorded for this election.

c051.text: From 1882 to 1886 Pennsylvania elected one member statewide (at-large). For the 1888 election that seat ended and all members were elected from redrawn districts.

c058.text: New map drawn after the 1900 census, which raised Pennsylvania's seats from 30 to 32. It was first used in the 1902 election.

c062.text: Not a new map: the historical boundary records show only slight differences in 3 districts from the previous Congress, and no statewide redistricting is recorded for this election.

c068.text: From 1912 to 1920 Pennsylvania elected four members statewide (at-large). For the 1922 election those seats ended and all 36 members were elected from districts.

c073.text: New map drawn after the 1930 census, which cut Pennsylvania's seats from 36 to 34. It was first used in the 1932 election.

c078.text: New map drawn after the 1940 census, which cut Pennsylvania's seats from 34 to 33. It was first used in the 1942 election.

c079.text: In 1942, after the 1940 census, Pennsylvania elected one member statewide (at-large). For the 1944 election that seat ended and all 33 members were elected from districts under a 1943 map.

c083.text: New map drawn after the 1950 census, which cut Pennsylvania's seats from 33 to 30. It was first used in the 1952 election.

c088.text: New map drawn after the 1960 census, which cut Pennsylvania's seats from 30 to 27. It was first used in the 1962 election.

c090.text: Pennsylvania's district lines were redrawn between censuses, first used in the 1966 election. The reason has not been researched yet.

c093.text: New map drawn after the 1970 census, which cut Pennsylvania's seats from 27 to 25. It was first used in the 1972 election.

c098.text: New map drawn after the 1980 census, which cut Pennsylvania's seats from 25 to 23. It was first used in the 1982 election.

c103.text: New map drawn after the 1990 census, which cut Pennsylvania's seats from 23 to 21. It was first used in the 1992 election.

c108.text: New map drawn after the 2000 census, which cut Pennsylvania's seats from 21 to 19. It was first used in the 2002 election.

c109.text: In April 2002 a federal court struck down the 2002 map over a 19-person population difference between districts but let it be used that year. The legislature passed a remedial plan (Act 34), which the court approved in January 2003.

c113.text: New map drawn after the 2010 census, which cut Pennsylvania's seats from 19 to 18. It was first used in the 2012 election.

c115.text: Not a new map: the historical boundary records show only slight differences in 5 districts from the previous Congress, and no statewide redistricting is recorded for this election.

c116.text: New map following: League of Women Voters v. Commonwealth. In January 2018 the Pennsylvania Supreme Court ruled that the 2011 congressional map violated the state constitution's Free and Equal Elections Clause. The court adopted its own map in February 2018, used from that year's election.

c118.text: New map following: Court picks a map. When the legislature and governor did not agree on a map, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court chose one in February 2022 in Carter v. Chapman.
